title: UnitedHealth's Q3 Margins Improve, But Membership Falls: Time to Buy? - TradingView
content: UnitedHealth Group Incorporated UNH showed further signs of a turnaround in the third quarter of 2026, with stronger earnings and improving profitability.Earnings beat expectations, medical costs eased, and management raised its annual outlook again. UNH shares jumped 7.4% since then. However, declining membership raises questions about whether the company can sustain its earnings recovery over the long term. UNH reported third-quarter adjusted earnings of $4.69 per share,beating the Zacks Consensus Estimate of $4.12 and rising 60.6% year over year.Revenues reached $112.7 billion, exceeding the consensus estimate by 1.2% but slipping from $113.2 billion last year. Operating earnings climbed to $6.6 billion from $4.3 billion, while net margin improved to 3.6% from 2.1%. The standout number was the medical care ratio, which measures the share of premium revenue spent on medical services. It fell to 88.4% from 89.9% a year ago. Even a modest improvement in this measure can have a large effect on earnings for an insurer of UnitedHealth's size. Lower claims pressure, tighter pricing and redesigned benefits helped drive the change. However, the quarter included $610 million of favorable medical reserve development related to 2026 care. Still, the operating cost ratio also improved to 12.8% from 13.5%, pointing to progress beyond claims alone. It again raised its 2026 adjusted earnings forecast to at least $20.50 per share from its previous $19.50-$20 range. For further details, see UNH Tops Q3 Earnings on Lower Medical Costs, Raises '26 Outlook. Are Better Margins Coming at the Expense of Growth? That is the central debate after earnings. UnitedHealthcare served 48.3 million people, down from 50.1 million a year ago. Medicare Advantage membership has fallen by 935,000 since the end of 2025 as the company withdrew from less attractive business and adjusted benefits. The financial payoff: UnitedHealthcare's operating profit increased to $2.8 billion from $1.8 billion despite lower revenue. Its operating margin climbed to 3.3% from 2.1%. Management now expects Medicare Advantage margins near the upper end of its 2-4% target range for 2026. Executives emphasized dual-eligible and chronic-condition plans alongside higher-value HMOs, rather than chasing enrollment across every product. More than 94% of Medicare-eligible Americans will have access to a UnitedHealthcare Medicare offering next year. A smaller, better-priced book seems healthier than growth that destroys profit. Still, a lasting turnaround requires enrollment to stabilize. Formal 2027 membership guidance remains ahead, making the upcoming selling season an important checkpoint. Optum offers another reason for optimism. Segment operating earnings rose to $3.7 billion from $2.5 billion even as revenue declined to $66.9 billion from $69.2 billion. Its margin expanded to 5.6% from 3.6%. Optum Health's turnaround was particularly notable. Operating earnings jumped to $735 million from just $41 million last year, with the margin reaching 3.2%. Revenue fell 10% as the business reduced exposure to markets where its value-based care operations lacked scale. Management expects further improvement in Optum Health's profitability in 2027 as it works toward its 6-8% margin target for 2028. Optum Insight's automation tools and Optum Rx's pharmacy operations offer additional earnings opportunities, but the company still must convert those initiatives into consistent growth. Optum Rx also faces pressure from lower prescription volumes tied to UnitedHealthcare's shrinking membership. Adjusted prescriptions declined to 393 million from 414 million. External customers now account for more than half its covered lives, however, reducing dependence on the insurance business. The Zacks Consensus Estimate for 2026 EPS is now pegged at $20.39, indicating 24.7% year-over-year growth. The earnings estimate has seen eight upward revisions over the past week against no downward movement. The consensus estimate for revenues is pegged at $447.4 billion, implying only a marginal decline from a year ago. For 2027, EPS is now projected to grow to $22.99, marking a 12.8% improvement. It has also seen seven upward estimate revisions in the past week, against no cuts. Revenues are pegged at $460.01 billion, indicating 2.8% growth from a year ago. The company beat earnings estimates in each of the past four quarters, producing an average earnings surprise of 14%. UnitedHealth Group Incorporated price-consensus-eps-surprise-chart | UnitedHealth Group Incorporated Quote Medical utilization remains the biggest uncertainty. Management said that commercial medical cost trends remain above 11%, although they have stabilized recently. Management expects core Medicaid margins to remain negative but better than negative 1% in 2026, with improvement anticipated in 2027. Medicare Advantage quality ratings add another challenge. For 2027, at least 69% of UnitedHealthcare's Medicare Advantage members are in plans rated four stars or higher, down from approximately 78% for 2026, per reports.Lower ratings can weigh on future bonus payments and product competitiveness. Nevertheless, UnitedHealth is targeting approximately 75% for 2028. Cash generation and debt also deserve attention. Operating cash flow totaled $5.1 billion in the quarter, or 1.2 times net income. Debt represented 41.7% of capital at September's end. The company aims to approach 40% by year-end while funding investments, dividends and repurchases. Looking at the year-to-date period, UNH stock has gained 23.2%, outperforming the S&P 500’s 12.9% rise, but trailing the industry’s 26% growth. Peers like Molina Healthcare, Inc. MOH and Centene Corporation CNC have increased 22.5% and 71.4%, respectively, during this time. Price Performance – UNH, MOH, CNC, Industry & S&P 500 UNH trades at 18.50X forward earnings, above the industry average of 16.08X but below its five-year median of 19.02X. In comparison, Molina and Centene are currently priced at 24.07X and 13.44X, respectively, both higher than their own five-year median multiples. Wall Street also sees room for further gains. Despite the stock’s recent rise, the average analyst price target of $476.52 suggests an upside of 17.2% from current levels. Individual targets range from $380 to $529, indicating that analysts remain divided over the pace and extent of UnitedHealth's recovery. UnitedHealth's stronger third-quarter earnings, improving margins and raised guidance suggest that its turnaround is moving in the right direction. Upward earnings estimate revisions add to the positive outlook. Although declining membership, elevated utilization and Medicare Advantage rating pressures remain concerns, management’s focus on profitable growth should help strengthen results over time. UNH's valuation remains below its historical median, while Optum's improving profitability provides another reason for optimism. Despite continued pressure from membership losses and elevated medical cost trends, the stock carries a Zacks Rank #2 (Buy), making it an attractive option for investors looking to benefit from the company's turnaround. Boeing is reportedly nearing a key FAA certification milestone for its smallest 737 MAX variant, the 737 Max 7, after years of delays that have disrupted airline fleet plans and slowed the company’s commercial recovery. BA shares edged up by about 0.5% after-hours on Thursday. The MAX 7 is expected to receive Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) approval later this month, The Wall Street Journal reported, citing people familiar with the matter. Southwest Airlines, with hundreds of orders for the jet, is expected to be the launch customer. An FAA spokesperson told WSJ that the safety approvals would dictate the timing of the MAX 7 certification. Boeing CEO Kelly Ortberg had predicted earlier this year that the jet would be approved by the end of 2026. The shorter, lighter MAX 7 is designed for shorter routes and offers better fuel efficiency than the older 737-700 it replaces. Together with the larger MAX 10, which competes directly with Airbus’s A321neo family, the two variants complete Boeing’s narrowbody lineup and represent a substantial portion of its undelivered backlog. Delays in the jet’s approval were caused by the 2018-2019 MAX grounding after two fatal crashes, the 2024 Alaska Airlines door-plug incident, and a long-running problem with the engine anti-ice system. Boeing only completed the anti-ice redesign in late 2025. The 737 MAX family is the core of Boeing’s commercial airplanes division and its main source of revenue and orders. Prolonged delays have limited deliveries, slowed cash flow, frustrated major customers, and allowed Airbus to gain ground in the single-aisle market. Since Kelly Ortberg became CEO in August 2024, Boeing has pursued an industrial reset focused on quality and production discipline. The company has strengthened oversight, reacquired fuselage supplier Spirit AeroSystems, and gradually raised output from 38 to 42 aircraft per month, with further increases planned. Certification of the MAX 7 and MAX 10 is viewed as essential to unlocking backlog value and supporting Boeing’s broader recovery. title: UnitedHealth Fell 51.32%, Then Rose 40.64%. DIA's Exposure Followed Both Moves by Design - 24/7 Wall St.
content: UnitedHealth's wild ride inside DIA was not an accident or a manager's call. The weighting rule baked into the Dow determined exactly how much of your money followed the stock up and down, and most investors have never read that… Read More: Learn 7 ways to generate income with a $1,000,000+ portfolio (sponsor) This post may contain links from our sponsors and affiliates, and Flywheel Publishing may receive compensation for actions taken through them. On November 11, 2024, UnitedHealth Group (NYSE:UNH | UNH Price Prediction) traded at $596.08. By May 30, 2025, it had fallen to $290.17, a 51.32% decline on a dividend-adjusted basis. From that bottom through October 15, 2026, the stock rose 40.64%. A delayed intraday quote on October 15, 2026, put it at $408.08, still below the November 2024 peak. If you own SPDR Dow Jones Industrial Average ETF (NYSEARCA:DIA), UnitedHealth’s share of your fund shrank and swelled along that entire path, driven solely by its share price. State Street Global Advisors describes DIA’s benchmark as a price-weighted index of 30 component common stocks. Price-weighted means one simple rule: the higher a stock’s share price, the bigger its slice of the fund. Company size, earnings, and business quality play no role. As UnitedHealth’s share price fell by half, its influence inside DIA fell with it. As the price climbed back, that influence returned automatically. The fund holds the most of a stock when it is most expensive and the least when it is cheapest. Those shifts come from the weighting rule alone. The relationship above follows directly from the published weighting method. State Street Global Advisors reports UnitedHealth at 4.55% of DIA as of October 14, 2026, making it the fund’s fifth-largest holding. State Street Global Advisors lists Goldman Sachs (NYSE:GS) as the largest position at 10.11% on the same date. Caterpillar (NYSE:CAT) ranks second at 8.62% and Microsoft (NASDAQ:MSFT) third at 6.14%.  The fourth-largest holding sits at 4.90%. Goldman leads because, under price weighting, the top position is by definition the highest-priced stock. That ranking reflects what one share costs. It says nothing about which business is largest or best run. These weights move every trading day with share prices. The rule that returned UnitedHealth’s role in the rebound also trimmed it on the way down. While the stock slipped from $596.08 to $290.17, DIA’s shrinking position limited the damage compared with a fund holding a fixed percentage. Price weighting cuts exposure to losers and adds exposure to risers. That helps in a sustained decline and hurts in a sharp rebound. Which effect wins depends entirely on the path a stock takes. The method has real strengths, too. The Dow carries an extremely long history, DIA is large and widely held, the methodology is published, and professionals understand it. No single holding wins the fund, so the effect on any one name stays limited. State Street Global Advisors lists DIA’s gross expense ratio at 0.16%, or $16 a year per $10,000 invested. Broad S&P 500 index funds charge as little as 0.03%, about $3 per $10,000. That gap compounds quietly, but it matters less than how the fund decides what you own. A market-cap-weighted fund sizes positions by total company value (share price times shares outstanding), which at least tracks something economic about the business. An equal-weight fund resets every holding to the same slice on a schedule, buying more of whatever has fallen. Price weighting instead follows the number printed on a single share, a number a stock split can cut overnight with no change to the underlying company. If you own DIA because the Dow sounds safe, note that, per State Street Global Advisors, share price alone determines how your money is allocated among its 30 stocks. UnitedHealth’s plunge and partial recovery show how that plays out on a real holding. Before you assume any fund’s largest positions reflect conviction or company size, check its weighting method. The University of New Hampshire welcomed 3,000 new students to its Durham and Manchester campuses this fall, representing a nearly 5 percent increase from last year’s incoming class. The university said the uptick in new students is bucking national trends. First-year undergraduate students at UNH increased 3.5 percent and transfer students increased 11.2 percent, compared with 2025 enrollment numbers. Other numbers from UNH about this fall’s new class: Incoming students posted an average high school GPA of 3.7 UNH awarded a record $40 million in financial aid to incoming students, with 96 percent of incoming students receiving aid. Out-of-state enrollment grew 11 percent, while in-state enrollment grew 1.7 percent. UNH said these figures reflect its “strengthened position in the New Hampshire market.” “While there are many challenges facing higher education right now, by focusing on a high-quality academic experience, experiential learning, and creating value for students and their families, we are increasingly a first-choice for many,” UNH President Elizabeth Chilton said in a news release Tuesday. Earlier this month, the University System of New Hampshire announced it would begin offering free tuition at the state’s public colleges to certain students beginning next year. Eligible students must be New Hampshire residents, meet certain academic requirements and be attending one of the schools for the first time. Their families cannot earn more than $100,000 a year. A UNH spokesperson estimated the change in eligibility requirements will mean an additional 29 percent of next year’s incoming class will qualify for the program.                         Kirsteen Mackay UnitedHealth raised its 2026 earnings outlook to at least $20.50 per adjusted share as third quarter results showed a lower medical care ratio and more profit. UnitedHealth's third quarter showed its cost controls are taking hold, as a lower medical care ratio helped lift operating earnings and supported a higher 2026 outlook. Gains came across UnitedHealthcare and Optum despite falling membership. Management sees 2027 growth near the low end of its long-term target, though medical costs, Medicaid funding and federal legal actions remain risks. UnitedHealth Group Inc. (NYSE: UNH) on October 13, 2026, raised its full year 2026 earnings outlook and now expects adjusted net earnings of at least $20.50 per share. The company said the forecast incorporates its experience through the third quarter 2026. On a GAAP basis, UnitedHealth now expects full year earnings of at least $19.50 per share. GAAP refers to standard US accounting rules, while the adjusted figure excludes items such as the amortization of acquired intangible assets and gains or losses tied to business sales. The updated outlook follows third quarter adjusted earnings of $4.69 per share, compared with $2.92 in the third quarter 2025. GAAP diluted earnings were $4.56 per share, up from $2.59 a year earlier. The release lists the Department of Justice's legal actions concerning UnitedHealth's participation in the Medicare program among the factors that could cause results to differ from expectations. It also cites changes in Medicare, the CMS star ratings program and risk adjustment data validation audits, which review the diagnosis data used to set government payments. UnitedHealth's medical care ratio, the share of premium revenue spent on patient care, was 88.4% in the third quarter, compared with 89.9% a year earlier. The company attributed the decline to medical cost management, benefit design changes and pricing. The ratio included $610 million of net favorable prior period reserve development related to 2026 dates of service. This means UnitedHealth's earlier estimates of claims owed for care delivered this year proved higher than the amounts now expected. Earnings from operations were $6.6 billion, compared with $4.3 billion in the third quarter 2025. The company said the increase was driven by execution across both its UnitedHealthcare insurance unit and its Optum health services unit. Consolidated revenue was $112.7 billion, compared with $113.2 billion a year earlier. Revenue in the second quarter 2026 was $112 billion. The operating cost ratio, which measures administrative costs against revenue, was 12.8%, compared with 13.5% in the third quarter 2025. The company said efficiency gains were partly offset by increased spending on technology, processes and staff. "Our third quarter results reflect the discipline and execution our teams are bringing to every part of our business," Stephen Hemsley, Chief Executive Officer, UnitedHealth Group, said in the earnings release. UnitedHealthcare earned $2.8 billion from operations in the quarter, up from $1.8 billion a year earlier, on revenue of $86.3 billion. The unit served 48.3 million people, compared with about 50.1 million at the end of the third quarter 2025. The number of seniors served through Medicare Advantage, including programs for complex populations also covered by Medicaid, has contracted by 935,000 since year-end 2025, according to the release. Optum Health revenue fell 10% to $22.9 billion. The company said it served fewer patients under value-based care, arrangements in which providers are paid based on patient outcomes and costs, in markets where it lacked enough presence to sustain its clinicians. Optum Health earnings from operations rose to $735 million from $41 million a year earlier. The company attributed the change to operational discipline and medical cost management in its value-based care markets. Optum Rx, the company's pharmacy benefits business, reported earnings from operations of $1.7 billion, compared with $1.5 billion a year earlier. Adjusted scripts fell to 393 million from 414 million, which the company linked to membership declines at UnitedHealthcare and other customers. Optum Insight, the data and technology unit, reported revenue of $5.5 billion, up 3% from a year earlier. Its earnings from operations rose to $1.3 billion from $920 million. On the earnings call, Tim Noel, who leads UnitedHealthcare, said commercial medical cost trends are running above the company's initial expectation of 11%. He cited costs tied to the No Surprises Act dispute process, greater cost intensity from clinicians and high-cost specialty drugs. The No Surprises Act is a federal law intended to protect patients from unexpected medical bills. Noel said arbitration awards under its dispute process can approach nearly 6% of total medical spending in some regions. Noel said UnitedHealth continues to view 2026 as a trough year for core Medicaid margins, which it now expects to be moderately better than negative 1%. He said the main variable remains the timing and adequacy of state funding. UnitedHealth's debt-to-capital ratio was 41.7% as of September 30, 2026, compared with 41.2% at the end of the second quarter. The company said it continues to target approximately 40% by year-end. The company repurchased $5 billion of its stock and paid $6.2 billion in dividends through the first nine months of 2026. Chief Financial Officer Wayne DeVeydt said the company expects dividends to exceed $8 billion by year-end. Management said it views the lower end of its 13% to 16% long-term growth target as a more reasonable starting point for 2027 and plans a fuller update in December, though elevated medical cost trends, government program funding and the Department of Justice's legal actions remain key risks to that outlook. title: UNH secures homecoming victory over Elon - The New Hampshire
content: October 3rd, 2026 marked the University of New Hampshire’s (UNH) 99th Homecoming Football Game, and the precedent was celebrated in style. The Wildcats (‘Cats) took home an impressive victory over Elon, winning 30-23 at Wildcat Stadium. Leading up to the much-anticipated homecoming match, seas of UNH students, alumni, family and friends poured into Boulder Field and A-lot. With Durham overflowing with spirit, and Wildcat stadium sold out, the ‘Cats did not disappoint. The first ‘Cats possession ended after 5 plays and a punt. This punt was bobbled by Elon’s returner, and picked up by ‘Cats receiver #17 Logan Perez. He brought the ball down to Elon’s 1-yard line, and the ‘Cats capitalized early in the first quarter with a 1-yard rushing touchdown from #11 Barry Kleinpeter. After the extra point was knocked in by #99 Logan Glassburn, the ‘Cats led by 7. Two possessions later, the ‘Cats marched down to the Elon 10-yard line, before having to settle for 3 points, the field goal was knocked in by Glassburn, 10-0 Wildcats. Elon answered with a field goal of their own, moving the score to 10-3. The final scoring act of the first quarter was claimed by UNH, as Logan Glassburn knocked in another field goal, giving the ‘Cats a 13-3 lead at the end of the first quarter. The ‘Cats conceded an early touchdown during Elon’s first drive of the second quarter,with the made extra point kick moving the score to 13-10. Elon’s quarterback threw a pair of interceptions to ‘Cats safeties in the second quarter: one to #12 Jackson Stone and the other to #10 Cohen Cook. UNH marched down the field on the final drive of the half, and Glassburn knocked in another field goal, moving the ‘Cats lead to 16-10. The ‘Cats first offensive possession of the second half yielded a 27-yard touchdown pass. UNH Quarterback #7 Brooks Bently threw a ball just short of the endzone to the open man #24 Joquez Smith, who turned and freely ran into the endzone. The extra point knocked in by Glassburn resulted in a 23-10 UNH lead. Elon answered with a touchdown of their own on the next possession, then promptly with a field goal, cutting the UNH lead down to 3, 23-20. The first drive of the 4th quarter for the ‘Cats yields a big pass from Bentley, caught by #88 Drew Danson, in the endzone for a UNH touchdown. Glassburn knocked in the extra point, and UNH led 30-23. Elon’s final score of the game came from a field goal, cutting the ‘Cats lead down to 4, 30-26. But it was too little, too late, and the ‘Cats took home the Homecoming victory. This week, the Wildcats take on Monmouth at Wildcat Stadium on October 17th, 2026.

title: UNH sees nearly 5% bump in enrollment; new students getting record financial aid - New Hampshire Public Radio
content: The University of New Hampshire welcomed 3,000 new students to its Durham and Manchester campuses this fall, representing a nearly 5% increase from last year’s incoming class. The university said the uptick in new students is bucking national trends. First-year undergraduate students at UNH increased 3.5% and transfer students increased 11.2%, compared with 2025 enrollment numbers. Other numbers from UNH about this fall’s new class: Out-of-state enrollment grew 11%, while in-state enrollment grew 1.7%. UNH said these figures reflect its “strengthened position in the New Hampshire market.” “While there are many challenges facing higher education right now, by focusing on a high-quality academic experience, experiential learning, and creating value for students and their families, we are increasingly a first-choice for many,” UNH President Elizabeth Chilton said in a news release Tuesday. Earlier this month, the University System of New Hampshire announced it would begin offering free tuition at the state’s public colleges to certain students beginning next year. Eligible students must be New Hampshire residents, meet certain academic requirements and be attending one of the schools for the first time. Their families cannot earn more than $100,000 a year. A UNH spokesperson estimated the change in eligibility requirements will mean an additional 29% of next year’s incoming class will qualify for the program. NHPR is nonprofit and independent. title: CNC, UNH, CVS, HUM Stocks Slip After-Hours — Trump Administration Reportedly Seeks To Scrap Subsidies On Certain Medicare Plans - Stocktwits
content: Shares of health insurance companies, including Centene (CNC), slipped after-hours on Tuesday following a report that the Trump administration plans to end a federal subsidy program that has helped suppress Medicare Part D prescription drug plan premiums. The federal program is currently channeling an estimated $3.6 billion to insurers this year to keep Part D premiums in check. Officials told The Wall Street Journal that the support will expire after 2026 and will not be extended into 2027. The Journal states that about 25 million Americans are enrolled in Part D plans, with the average monthly premium this year running near $36. The Wall Street Journal reports the decision could leave many seniors confronting higher premiums for their stand-alone prescription coverage beginning in 2027. Without the federal support, plan sponsors may pass increased costs to enrollees, potentially accelerating shifts toward Medicare Advantage plans that bundle drug benefits. An administration official quoted by the Journal projected that roughly one-quarter of Part D enrollees will see their premiums hold steady or decline in 2027, about 30% will face hikes under $10 a month, and the remaining 45% will largely see increases in the $11–$20 range. The subsidy primarily benefits insurers offering stand-alone Part D plans (PDPs). Companies with substantial PDP enrollment—UnitedHealth Group (UNH), CVS Health (CVS, via Aetna), Humana (HUM), Centene (CNC, via WellCare), and Molina Healthcare (MOH)—stand to lose this revenue stream. Loss of the $3.6-billion in support could pressure margins if insurers absorb costs or reduce competitiveness through higher premiums, risking enrollment declines. However, beneficiaries might also migrate to Medicare Advantage plans and help offset losses. Centene holds the largest share of stand-alone Medicare Part D (PDP) enrollment via Wellcare — more than eight million members as of early 2026, or about one-third of the entire PDP market, exceeding the exposure of its rivals. CNC shares dived 3% after hours on Tuesday, while shares of UNH, CVS, and HUM fell by about or less than 1%. On Stocktwits, retail sentiment around CNC jumped from ‘bearish’ to ‘bullish’ territory over the past 24 hours, while message volume rose from ‘normal’ to ‘high’ levels. In a major bid to accelerate American dominance in the commercial space sector, the Trump administration announced a proposal allowing the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) to bypass lengthy environmental reviews for rocket launches, spacecraft reentries, and commercial launch site approvals. The initiative, announced on Tuesday by Transportation Secretary Sean P. Duffy, aims to eliminate red tape for commercial operators as the U.S. prepares for an unprecedented surge in orbital launches and space infrastructure development. Commercial space stocks, including Rocket Lab (RKLB), AST SpaceMobile (ASTS), Intuitive Machines (LUNR), and Planet Labs (PL) dropped between 3% and 7% on Tuesday, while SpaceX (SPCX) added 3%. Under the proposed framework, the FAA would gain the authority to waive requirements established across 13 major federal environmental statutes. These include the National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA), the Endangered Species Act, the Clean Water Act, and the Clean Air Act. Federal officials emphasized that exemptions would only apply where environmental rules delay innovation, maintaining that core public health, national security, and safety safeguards will remain intact. "America won the first Space Race, and we can do it again -- but only if we get government red tape out of the way," Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy stated, noting that the goal is to lower costs and strengthen U.S. competitiveness. Environmental assessments—which currently can take over a year to complete—have long been a target of frustration for commercial launch providers. While conservation groups view these evaluations as crucial for protecting coastal wildlife habitats, launch companies have repeatedly slammed the reviews as duplicative administrative bottlenecks. The FAA's proposal opens a 30-day public comment window before final rules are enacted. The drive to deregulate comes as the commercial space industry experiences exponential growth. The FAA reported authorizing a record 204 commercial space operations in FY2025. Over the next decade, federal forecasts project total operations could reach over 4,200, climbing from 214 this year to more than 500 annual operations by 2036. Much of this growth is being driven by heavyweights like Elon Musk’s SpaceX, Jeff Bezos’ Blue Origin, Rocket Lab, and rising startups like Stoke Space. These firms are aggressively deploying satellite constellations for broadband connectivity, defense applications, and orbital data centers. Rocket Lab (RKLB) made massive waves in the market after announcing an $8-billion acquisition of Iridium Communications. The deal hands Rocket Lab an operational 66-satellite network, global L-band spectrum, and 2.55 million active subscribers, firmly establishing it as the primary commercial competitor to SpaceX. AST SpaceMobile (ASTS) confirmed its next-generation BlueBird 8, 9, and 10 satellites are fully operational in orbit, while SpaceX recently cleared its FAA mishap investigation for Starship Flight 12, paving the way for Flight 13 as it prepares for up to 44 orbital launches annually from NASA's Kennedy Space Center in Florida. According to a filing with the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission on Tuesday, the prince now beneficially owns 19.5 million shares of Lucid’s Class A common stock. The prince’s spokesperson reportedly told Bloomberg that the purchases were made during a recent slump in LCID’s share price. Lucid, based in California, already maintains close links to Saudi Arabia through its majority shareholder, the Public Investment Fund. PIF holds a majority stake of around 57% in Lucid Group, according to a company filing from late April. The stake is held primarily through Ayar Third Investment Company, a wholly owned PIF subsidiary. Earlier this month, Lucid rejected reports that it was considering bankruptcy or a take-private transaction, noting that it has sufficient liquidity to carry its operations well into next year. The company also delivered a cease and desist letter to the publication that carried the bankruptcy rumors, stating that the company “unequivocally denies the central factual assertions” in the article. Lucid is now slated to provide a further update on its financials in its second-quarter earnings call scheduled for August 4. The company, however, has faced significant headwinds. Earlier this month, the company reported second-quarter production of 4,774 vehicles and deliveries of 3,953 units— marking a modest year-over-year increase but short of analyst expectations amid slower-than-hoped demand for the new Gravity SUV. Financially, Lucid continues to face steep losses and negative gross margins despite revenue growth. The company is currently attempting to ramp up growth under the leadership of CEO Silvio Napoli, who assumed the role in June. Napoli undertook a leadership overhaul recently and replaced CFO Taoufiq Boussaid with automotive finance veteran Alexander De Bock. He also appointed new executives for technology, customer, digital, and transformation roles, flattened the reporting structure by halving direct reports to the CEO, and eliminated the COO position. These moves followed June layoffs of roughly 1,500 employees, about 18% of the workforce, and the removal of a second production shift at the Arizona plant, aimed at delivering roughly $158 million in annual savings. The company has relied heavily on its PIF for support through it all. In late April 2026, Ayar purchased $550 million of Lucid’s Series C convertible preferred stock and expanded Lucid’s delayed-draw term loan facility by $500 million. Most recently, on July 6, Lucid drew $800 million under those existing facilities, converting committed credit into immediate cash. title: UNH Stock Outpaces S&P 500 In 2026, Eyes Best Year Since Pandemic — CFO Says Wall Street May Be Missing 2027 Upside - TradingView
content: Shares of UnitedHealth (UNH) have outpaced the S&P 500 so far in 2026 and are on pace for their strongest year since 2021. Now, CFO Wayne DeVeydt says Wall Street may be underestimating the company’s earnings opportunity in 2027. UNH stock is up nearly 17% in 2026, outpacing the S&P 500’s 14% gain and the Health Care Select Sector SPDR Fund’s (XLV) 11% rise. The rebound follows a 33% plunge last year. UnitedHealth reported third-quarter (Q3) adjusted earnings of $4.69 per share, topping the $4.14 analyst consensus. Revenue also beat estimates, coming in at $112.69 billion on $111.49 billion, though it was slightly below the $113.2 billion reported a year earlier. Earnings from operations climbed to $6.6 billion from $4.3 billion. The company raised its 2026 adjusted earnings outlook to at least $20.50 per share, from a previous range of $19.50 to $20. But even after its recent rebound, UNH shares are up just 19% since January 2021, a 3% annualized gain over nearly six years. “Current analyst consensus for 2027 may understate the opportunity ahead,” DeVeydt said on the earnings call. He added, “The quality of earnings is strong and durable as we head into 2027.” He called the lower end of UnitedHealth’s long-term adjusted earnings growth target of 13% to 16% a “reasonable starting point.” By Stocktwits’ calculation, 13% growth on the $20.50 floor would imply about $23.17 a share in 2027. Analysts’ quarterly estimates compiled by Fiscal.ai sum to about $22.80. DeVeydt cited share repurchases, value-based care, enterprise-wide progress and gains from artificial intelligence and modernization as potential tailwinds. He also flagged policy reforms, modernization spending, medical-cost trends and pressure on health-benefit funding as headwinds. Quarterly revenue climbed 61% from $70.2 billion in the first quarter of 2021 to $112.7 billion in the third quarter of 2026. Operating profit, however, was nearly unchanged, slipping from $6.7 billion to $6.6 billion. Revenue hovered around $112 billion in the second and third quarters of 2026, while earnings per share swung more sharply. Basic EPS fell to nearly zero in the fourth quarter of 2025, rebounded to $6.90 in the first quarter of 2026, then declined to $6.10 in the second quarter and $4.60 in the third. UnitedHealth reported adjusted EPS of $2.11 for the fourth quarter of 2025. Analysts estimate basic EPS will peak at $8.20 in the first quarter of 2027, then fall to $6.90 in the second quarter, $4.80 in the third and $2.90 in the fourth, according to Fiscal.ai. UnitedHealth’s average 12-month analyst price target is $480.68, implying about 27% upside from current levels. Of 26 analysts, 7 rate the stock ‘Strong Buy,’ 15 ‘Buy’ and 4 ‘Hold’; none rate it ‘Sell’ or ‘Strong Sell,’ according to Koyfin. UNH’s Medicare Advantage Recovery Faces Membership Test UnitedHealth’s medical care ratio fell to 88.4% in the third quarter from 89.9% a year earlier, reflecting tighter pricing, benefit changes and cost controls. The result also included $610 million in favorable reserve development. But the ratio rose from 86.7% in the second quarter, and commercial medical trends remained above 11%. When asked whether the trends were worsening, UnitedHealthcare CEO Tim Noel said, “We are not seeing the dynamics that you are talking about.” Medicaid is another pressure point. UnitedHealth expects 2026 to be a trough year for core Medicaid margins, which it now projects to be moderately better than negative 1%. The firm expects margins to return to targeted levels by the end of 2028. At least 69% of UnitedHealthcare’s Medicare Advantage members are in plans rated four stars or higher in the 2027 star ratings, which affect bonus payments in 2028. The company expects that share to reach 75% as it moves through 2027 and into 2028, compared with a 70% industry average. The company plans to focus on high-value Health Maintenance Organization (HMO) plans and special-needs plans for people with chronic conditions or who qualify for both Medicare and Medicaid. UnitedHealthcare is UnitedHealth’s revenue heavyweight, bringing in $86.3 billion in the third quarter. It provides health coverage to employers and individuals and runs the company’s Medicare Advantage and Medicaid plans. Revenue dipped from $87.1 billion a year earlier, but operating earnings climbed to $2.8 billion from $1.8 billion. Optum is the group’s health-services engine. Optum Health delivers care and manages provider networks. Optum Rx handles pharmacy services and prescription benefits. Optum Insight provides tech and data services to healthcare organizations. Together, the businesses generated $66.9 billion in revenue and $3.7 billion in operating earnings. Optum Health’s earnings surged to $735 million from $41 million, while Optum Rx said external clients made up more than half its membership for the first time. Retention remained in the high 90s. Operator: Good morning, and welcome to the UnitedHealth Group third quarter 2026 earnings conference call. A question and answer session will follow UnitedHealth Group's prepared remarks. As a reminder, this call is being recorded. Here is some important introductory information. This call contains forward-looking statements under U.S. federal securities laws. These statements are subject to risks and uncertainties that could cause actual results to differ materially from historical experience or present expectations. A description of some of the risks and uncertainties can be found in the reports that we file with the Securities and Exchange Commission, including the cautionary statements included in our current and periodic filings. This call will also reference non-GAAP amounts. A reconciliation of the non-GAAP to GAAP amounts is available on the financial and earnings reports section of the company's investor relations page at www.unitedhealthgroup.com. Information presented on this call is contained in the earnings release we issued this morning and in our Form 8-K, dated October 13, 2026, which may be accessed from the investor relations page of the company's website. I will now turn the conference over to Chairman and Chief Executive Officer of UnitedHealth Group, Steve Hemsley. Steve Hemsley: Good morning, and thank you for joining us today. Our third quarter performance reflects actions taken throughout 2026, driving meaningful progress and reinforcing our confidence to sustainably grow in 2027 and beyond within our 13%-16% long-term target growth range. Our revised full year 2026 guidance reflects continuing improvements in leadership and execution across Optum and UnitedHealthcare as we better align our businesses to serve the demands of the ever-changing U.S. healthcare environment. We are accelerating the modernization of our enterprise by advancing simplified and more responsive policies, processes, and tools, focusing on more effective integrated value-based care offerings, and responsibly building modern agentic infrastructure as we seek to ensure people have access to higher quality care at lower costs, and at the same time, clinicians experience a simpler, faster, and more supportive system. Across the businesses, AI-enabled capabilities are beginning to help clinicians spend more time with patients, improve service speed and experience, streamline administration, and reduce friction for both consumers and clinicians. A few examples. We have expanded AI-enabled chart summarization to more than 40% of our employed clinicians, reducing chart review time by 33%. AI-enabled information gathering and research have shortened appeal cycle times by 26%, improving both member and clinician experience, and we expect this to accelerate in 2027. For this year's Medicare Advantage annual enrollment period, we are introducing AI-powered plan recommendation that use a member's care history and local plan options to help simplify their selection. By the end of this year, we are on track to implement all previously announced prior authorization reforms, reducing decision timelines for patients, relieving administrative burden for clinicians, and delivering better experiences for people. Collectively, these initiatives will reduce total prior authorizations by 30%, including a reduction of two-thirds in prior authorizations for people under the age 18. These efforts are only the beginning. More will follow. They are central to how we're changing our enterprise to be more in line with our mission, creating greater value and positive social impact. In that vein, an important effort is the reimagined United Health Foundation. With $1 billion committed to date, the foundation's investments, along with the dedicated operational expertise of UnitedHealthcare and Optum, can help facilitate scaled solutions to some of the U.S. health system's greatest challenges, including rural health, maternal and infant health, behavioral health, and workforce education. As just one example, in Tennessee, the foundation is helping expand and operate health hubs across the state, providing access to underserved communities in preventative care and chronic condition support. We will continue to highlight the foundation as part of our commentary on our earnings calls going forward. The broader healthcare environment remains dynamic. Policy-driven regulatory developments, changing consumer expectations, and the rapid evolution of clinical care and advances in technology continue to reshape the industry. These factors are pressuring basic affordability and access as never before. Success requires continuous adaptation, and the pace is accelerating. We recognize this and remain restless in our pursuit of change and improvement. We are challenging our assumptions, revising policies and practices, and repositioning leadership and capabilities to better meet the needs of those we serve and to move faster as an enterprise to adapt to the changing healthcare landscape. That includes opportunities to better align with clinical partners, employers, government benefit sponsors to help improve the experience of all stakeholders in healthcare. We've made progress in our 2026 performance. We have much to do to approach the full potential of our mission and the positive impact we can make as an enterprise. UnitedHealth Group has a long history of evolution to meet the needs of a changing U.S. health system. We're committed to accelerating these efforts as a stronger, more capable, more mission-centered enterprise. With that, let me turn the call over to Tim Noel. Tim Noel: Thanks, Steve. UnitedHealthcare is seeing positive momentum across our Medicare and Medicaid businesses. While our commercial business continues to adjust to a challenging but steadily stabilizing environment. Costs remain stubbornly high across the entire healthcare landscape, and particularly in areas such as specialty pharmacy and acute healthcare service intensity. We continue to address the challenge of increasingly expensive care with appropriate medical management, operational discipline, and a commitment to identify and remove excess and unnecessary costs from our own enterprise as we advance simpler and more modern services. We are working to deliver stable benefits and value for our members and customers. We believe this positions us for continued organic growth and long-term value creation entering 2027. Let me start with our Medicare business, where the annual enrollment period begins later this week. Medicare Advantage remains the choice of well more than half of eligible American seniors as it offers better and more modern benefits, and importantly, better outcomes than fee-for-service Medicare. Beneficiaries choosing Medicare Advantage save on average more than $4,000 annually through lower premiums and cost sharing than those on original Medicare. With adequate funding, we believe Medicare Advantage will continue to be the choice of American seniors, particularly those who are disadvantaged and have chronic care challenges as they seek better value and modern care. Heading into 2026, we made deliberate decisions regarding Medicare Advantage benefit design and market positioning to preserve the long-term sustainability and performance of our Medicare Advantage offerings. We continued this disciplined approach for 2027. We believe we are competitively positioned, focused on providing value for seniors in the markets we serve while being mindful of trend dynamics. In 2027, UnitedHealthcare will continue to prioritize high-value HMO, chronic special needs, and dual special needs offerings. Our commitment to serving America's seniors is clear. More than 94% of Medicare-eligible individuals nationwide will have access to a UnitedHealthcare Medicare plan, and approximately 90% of Medicare-eligible consumers will have access to one of our Medicare Advantage plans with a $0 premium option. We are maintaining important benefits such as dental, vision, hearing, and additional health and wellness offerings that make a real difference in the lives of seniors. UnitedHealthcare chronic special needs plans will be available to nearly 50 million Medicare-eligible individuals in 2027, providing specialized support for people living with conditions such as diabetes, cardiovascular disease, and chronic heart failure. These plans offer benefits and access to care tailored to the unique needs of individuals managing chronic conditions, helping them connect with care, medications, and support they need. Much of this work is in coordination with our partners at Optum Health, where evidence shows chronically complex seniors served by integrated value-based care experience better preventative care while improving health outcomes at lower costs. Medicare Advantage patients in value-based care arrangements are 40% likely than traditional Medicare patients to be hospitalized for acute and chronic conditions, and 40% less likely to be readmitted to a hospital within 30 days of discharge. Moving to Stars. Our initial Star Ratings for payment year 2028 reflect our investment in quality, member experience, and operating execution. As we move through 2027 and into 2028, we expect to approach 75% of total members in four-plus Star plans compared to the industry average of 70%. Our team remains intensely focused on building a best-in-class consumer and clinical experience. Along with better benefit design and stability going forward, we believe those efforts will continue translating into stronger quality performance over time. We will continue to work in support of the CMS quality program efforts to ensure the Medicare Advantage program continues to provide quality experience and stability to the 36 million seniors who depend on it. Turning to medical costs. The actions we've taken to improve and modernize care management, strengthen clinical engagement, and enhance operating discipline are having a meaningful effect. Care intensity remains elevated relative to historical norms, even as we continue to see signs that trends are bending in a more stable direction than what we have recently experienced. We remain respectful of trends, and are not assuming any deceleration to historical patterns or to ongoing clinician pricing pressure. Demand for care remains strong, particularly among senior and complex populations, and we fully support appropriate access to care for our members. Turning to the commercial business. Performance continues to stabilize as we navigate a challenging market. As we previously noted, trends for commercial benefits are exceeding our initial expectations of 11%, driven by an acceleration of costs related to the No Surprises Act, greater cost intensity from clinicians, and high-cost specialty drugs. Of particular concern is the ongoing abuse of the No Surprises Act dispute process by a relatively small number of clinician groups and third-party organizations. Arbitration awards can approach nearly 6% of total medical spend in some regions, translating to billions of dollars in excess costs for consumers, employers, and the health system. The law was intended to protect patients from unexpected bills, and we strongly support that objective. We will continue working with policymakers and regulators to ensure the law functions as intended and that healthcare dollars are directed towards appropriate patient care rather than significantly inflated market arbitration awards and volumes, along with unnecessary administrative expense. Medicaid remains stable through the back half of the year, while our team continues to drive greater operational improvements through network curation and more effective behavioral health program initiatives. These actions help to partially offset the primary variable, which continues to be the timing and adequacy of state funding across several markets. As we move through the balance of 2026, we continue to work collaboratively with our state partners to ensure rates appropriately reflect the acuity and healthcare needs of the families being served, including the impacts of regulatory actions. While progress has been made in many states, the timing of updates remains uneven. Based on our current outlook, we continue to view 2026 as a trough year for core Medicaid margins, which we now expect to be moderately better than negative 1%. Finally, we are focusing intensely on enhancing our support for, and relationships with, clinicians and health systems. In addition to the prior authorization changes Steve mentioned, which we see as only the beginning, we are meaningfully speeding up our claims processing and payments, and re-energizing our relationship engagement efforts with more dedicated resources and executive ownership. Our goal is to provide a more seamless experience for clinicians and health systems who work with us and to resolve issues more quickly. As we look towards 2027 and beyond, we are shifting our focus to sustainable organic growth underpinned by improving Medicare fundamentals, a stronger commercial outlook, continued opportunities to enhance Medicaid performance, and an organization that is operating with greater discipline and accountability for all our stakeholders. With that, I'll turn it over to Patrick. Patrick Conway: Thanks, Tim. Our results from the third quarter underscore the important work underway across all of Optum to lay the groundwork for long-term growth. Starting with Optum Health. Overall, Optum Health continued to deliver strong performance in the third quarter, driven by the continued return to value-based care principles, combined with strong execution across our clinical programs and operational improvements, enabling clinicians to focus more on their patients and improve patient experience. A few of the examples for this morning, a 27% increase from last year in online self-scheduling, making it easier for patients to reach clinicians. An increase in home health visits by 10% over last year. We are very encouraged by the early success of our program to co-locate behavioral specialists within our primary care practices. The number of patients referred has doubled since last year, with an engagement rate of more than 90%. As Tim mentioned, it is now more important than ever to provide seamless care and coverage for our chronic and complex patients through all phases of the care continuum, from primary care to specialist, to home to the pharmacy. Moving to Optum Rx. Our focus in this business continues to be on two efforts to ensure value alignment to the customers and patients we serve. First, we continue to increase transparency on the PBM side of Optum Rx. Through the 2027 selling season, we have seen our industry-first affordability, experience, and transparency initiatives resonating in the marketplace and customers. The employers, governments, unions we serve continuing to recognize the vital role of PBMs in controlling prescription drug costs and ensuring people have access to the medications they need, particularly as the prices charged by drug manufacturers continue to increase. For the first time, over 50% of Optum Rx membership is external, non-UHC membership. Second, we fundamentally believe that pharmacy services have to be closer to the patient. Accordingly, you will see continued efforts within our separate pharmacy services businesses to more closely align pharmacy care with medical care. Integrated value-based care means just that, integrated. When pharmacy care and medical care are aligned, outcomes improve for the patients we serve, access improves, and the total cost of care is lowered. Specifically, within the pharmacy service side of Optum Rx, Genoa continues to expand its dedicated behavioral health pharmacy footprint and serve patients with serious mental illness and substance use disorders. Specialty pharmacy continues to grow through both volume and mix while improving patient support for increasingly complex therapies. Infusion services are becoming more important as we help shift appropriate care into lower cost and more convenient settings. We will continue to expand our portfolio of integrated pharmacy services and align them as close to medical care settings as possible, delivering better care, convenience, and access. Turning to Optum Insight. 2026 has been both a performance and an investment year, and 2027 will show meaningful progress, setting the foundation for accelerating growth in 2028 and beyond. Our investment focus has been on further developing and bringing to market healthcare-specific AI solutions that enhance productivity performance outcomes while improving the patient and clinician experience. Overall, we are looking to 2027 with confidence. Our major remediation work is largely complete, and it's created a strong foundation for growth across Optum. With that, I'll turn it over to Wayne. Wayne DeVeydt: Thanks, Patrick, and good morning. Third quarter results reflect continued progress across the enterprise and improving execution in our businesses where we have been focused on operating reforms to drive better consumer and clinician experience. For Q3 2026, we reported revenue of $113 billion and adjusted earnings per share of $4.69, up from $2.92 a year ago. Consolidated medical care ratio of 88.4% for the quarter compares to 89.9% last year. The quality of earnings is strong and durable as we head into 2027. At UnitedHealthcare, performance continued to reflect pricing discipline, fundamental medical cost management, and care delivery enhancements. We continue to be respectful of continued elevated utilization trends, which typically step up in the back half of the year, particularly in our risk-based businesses. Within Optum Health, we are seeing steady progress from modernization, a return to a disciplined value-based care approach, and operating improvements as the actions taken through 2026 begin to yield results. In Optum Insight, performance is benefiting from technology and AI-enabled improvements, including payment integrity and broader operating efficiency while we invest into the new areas to expand and modernize our offerings to drive growth. In Optum Rx, we continue to see the benefits of disciplined execution and the breadth of our pharmacy services model now based on a simpler, more transparent approach to serving these evolving market needs. Turning to the full year, our updated 2026 adjusted EPS guidance of at least $20.50 reflects performance through the third quarter, balanced by expected investments in the final months of the year. From a capital deployment perspective, our priorities remain consistent. First, reinvest in the business through targeted organic growth and steady expansion in care delivery, technology, modernization, and broad-based AI adoption. Second, maintain balance sheet strength. Third, return value to shareholders. Our balance sheet remains strong. Our debt-to-cap ratio was 41.7% at the close of the quarter, and we remain on track to approach 40% by year-end. We repurchased $5 billion of UNH stock through the third quarter. We have paid $6.2 billion in dividends year to date and expect to exceed $8 billion by year-end. Our strategic priorities remain focused on capabilities that align with and strengthen our ability to deliver value to consumers, benefit sponsors, and customers and support long-term growth for shareholders. We view our 2026 adjusted EPS guidance of at least $20.50 as a solid run rate on which to grow. We would offer that current analyst consensus for 2027 may understate the opportunity ahead, and we see the lower end of our long-term 13%-16% growth rate as a more reasonable starting point. As we think about 2027 more broadly, we continue to see a balanced set of tailwinds and headwinds. Tailwinds include continued enterprise-level performance progress, share repurchases, value-based care performance improvements, and further gains from AI and modernization that improve both consumer and clinician experiences, drive productivity benefits, reduce costs, and create sustainable performance improvement opportunities for our business and those we serve, as well as product opportunities for Optum Insight. On the headwind side, we will accelerate our investments in the policy reforms and modernization of the businesses, particularly in UnitedHealthcare and Optum Insight, and remain respectful of medical trends and the broader external environment where health benefit funding remains pressured. Overall, we're steadily and methodically improving performance broadly across the portfolio. We are positioned to finish 2026 strongly, and we remain focused on consistently delivering our 13%-16% long-term growth target. With that, I'll turn it back over to Wayne. Steve Hemsley: Thanks, Wayne. Let me close with a few thoughts before we move to questions. For a little more than a year, our priorities have been clear. Return to our core mission and culture. Better serve the needs of healthcare as one enterprise and one leadership team. Restore financial and operating discipline. Turn around and strengthen our performance business by business across all performance measures. Begin the process of reimagining and modernizing all we do to harness the compelling potential of modern intelligent technologies. Simplify our processes, elevate our service levels, and advance our response and service speed to consumers and clinicians. Finally, reposition all our businesses to return to responsible levels of profitable organic growth. As you've heard today, we are well underway in all those areas. But fully achieving those priorities requires us to get outside our four walls. Throughout our company, we are spending time listening carefully to customers, consumers, clinicians, policymakers, and other stakeholders. We're doing so with humility and with a service mindset, conscious of the positive role we can play and the responsibility we have to improve the health system experience when we operate at our best. Those conversations are helping renew and reinforce the fundamental understanding that success in healthcare depends on relationships and trust, and we need to continue to build both with all stakeholders. We will continue listening, we will continue learning, and we will continue advancing our business in ways that improve experiences, provide easier access, and lower costs while delivering better outcomes. For you, our shareholders, all these accountabilities align and create value. The progress we've made in 2026 gives us confidence. Our businesses are improving. Our modernization efforts are gaining traction. Our investments in AI and in integrated value-based care are creating tangible benefits today while positioning us for the future. We remain focused on better managing our businesses, finishing 2026 strong, and building that foundation for growth in 2027 and 2028 and beyond. We look forward to providing you more comprehensive update on our outlook for next year before year-end. I will thank you now and the operator, let's open the line for questions. Operator: The floor is now open for questions. At this time, if you have a question or comment, please press star one on your touch tone phone. You may remove yourself from the queue by pressing star two on your touch tone phone. We ask you to limit yourself to one question. If you ask multiple questions, we will only be answering the first question so that we can respond to everyone in the queue this morning. Our first question comes from Justin Lake with Wolfe Research. Justin Lake: Thanks. Good morning. I wanted to focus on the government side for a second, specifically your comments around Medicaid. Things were getting better. I am curious what you are seeing in terms of your third quarter run rate and what is driving that. Are you actually back to kind of break even given your improvement there? Maybe you can also let us know where your MA margins are at this point for 2026. Thanks. Mike: Sure. Thanks, Justin. Good morning, and thank you for the question. As Tim Noel indicated, our membership and overall Q here are within our expectations, and we now expect full 2026 performance moderately better than our forecasted range. The main drivers of that activity has really been our focus on complex care cost management, network and services curation, increasing our membership engagement, particularly in our coaching AI power coaching activities, modernization activities, and the ongoing identification and removal of fraud, waste, and abuse activities. We do believe these activities are doable. We did see good improvement in Q3, and we believe that will continue on for the rest of the year. We continue to see elevated trends in the areas of behavioral healthcare services, specialty pharmacy services, and home and community-based services, and also in inpatient care costs as well. Those elevation rates are moderating slightly, and we're continuing to monitor that. We anticipate margin improvement as we look into next year, and we will continue to work with our state partners to mitigate what has been a stubborn gap between funding and medical cost trends through the year. Again, as we think about this for 2028, we're very aspirational to move to targeted margins by the end of that year. Thank you for the question. Bobby Hunter: Hey, Justin, maybe this is Bobby on the Medicare margin piece that you highlighted. Given where we've paced through 2026, we do now expect to be near the top end of the 2%-4% range. I would attribute a lot of that to some of the great recovery actions that the team has executed on here throughout the year. Think the initiatives around medical trend, our cost management focus, and then a broader focus on the durable product offerings that we've brought to the marketplace for 2026. It also allows us to make investments now to set us up for future success. Think what we're doing in quality, what we're doing in AI, modernization, provider. Ultimately, I feel good about how it sets us up for continued success in 2027. Thanks for the question. Operator: Our next question comes from Lance Wilkes with Bernstein. Lance Wilkes: Great. Could you talk a little bit about how you are approaching growth in 2027, in particular in Medicare Advantage as you are approaching the top end of the range, how you are looking at growth there? Likewise, with the selling seasons in for national accounts and for PBM, how is that coming along? Bobby Hunter: Yep. Yeah. Hey, thanks, Lance, for the question. Yes, AEP right around the corner here. We will wait till later this year to provide formal membership guidance. Maybe a couple early observations to share with you. Obviously, some of the things we did as we set out for planning in 2027 was continue to look at ensuring we have a durable set of product offerings, and that meant some continued footprint refinements and product refinements really around the residual PPOs that we started moderating a year or two ago. Then as I look at the opportunities, I think that is actually a lot of good growth potential out there. Maybe one important stat for you, even with some of the footprint refinements, we did actually expand our overall footprint. Tim noted it in the prepared remarks. Now more than 94% of American eligibles for Medicare have access to one of our plan offerings. That is an expansion year-over-year. We also took a more dynamic approach to the product planning this year, and I think there are some real opportunities for smart, durable growth in the marketplace right now. We are particularly focused on the D-SNP offerings, the C-SNP offerings, and then some of the high-value HMO. I think we are better positioned to capture that growth in some of those key areas as we step into AEP in 2027 than we have been in recent years, and we aligned our go-to-market strategy accordingly. Maybe just last thing to highlight on that is when I think about the overall capabilities of the enterprise, the capabilities that we bring to bear, our emphasis on value-based care, I do think we have an incredible opportunity to make an impact for the members that are on these D-SNP, C-SNP, and HMO plans, and really drive some incredible outcomes and quality for those folks over time. Tim Noel: Yeah. Lance, this is Tim Noel.
